title: Education and daycare are different
author: Educating Hatbeasts
summary: This home-education post uses a single afternoon, when a nine-year-old suddenly demanded to solve a cubic equation with Cardano's Method, to ask what tutors are actually for. The author, a parent with strong maths qualifications, could not help, and neither could the part-time facilitator, so the child's father taught the method on his lunch break. She then surveys parents of children with council-funded education outside school and finds two main kinds of tuition: structured academic coaching, which suits bright children who cannot attend school poorly, and unstructured learning that often works like respite care. Neither type fits a child who asks an advanced question in an unpredictable subject at an unpredictable moment. She sympathizes with parents who cannot teach beyond their own level and argues that education and daycare should be kept clearly separate.
points: A child's spontaneous, advanced questions expose a gap that neither parents nor generalist facilitators nor standard tuition models are built to fill.
Structured, worksheet-style tuition tends to fail the very bright children who could not manage school, while unstructured tuition often functions as respite care.
The assumption that parents can always educate their own children is a privilege that many families, especially those with SEND children, do not have.
One suggested model is an on-call pool of subject experts who answer children's saved-up questions without compliance pressure.
The author argues for separating cheaper daycare from more formal academic teaching.
quotes: Most long-time home educators don’t see the point. They see kids as being able to learn everything they need from a parent (plus books, etc.).
The problem is that Bigger Boy is spontaneously rocking up with questions that are above GCSE, in multiple subjects
If you feel you don’t know enough to educate your own child, why are you such a fan of school-like learning? After all, it didn’t work for you
There’s a certain privilege in assuming parents can always educate their own kids.
The first is very structured and academic, which tends not to work well with bright kids who can’t access schools. If they thrived completing worksheets, they probably would be still there.
The second is unstructured learning, often with the aim of getting the child to eventually engage with more formal learning.
If kids’ save up their burning questions about Cardano’s Method, at some point an adult will show up to help them solve it, but not in a way that’s compliance-based or lacking in their consent.
It also clearly separates daycare (which is cheaper) from more formalised academic learning.
